summary: Kole Jain walks through seven beginner UI/UX mistakes, plus a bonus one on charts, by fixing a simple recipe app one mistake at a time instead of redesigning it from scratch. The mistakes are an unplanned user flow, overused effects (gradients and harsh drop shadows), cramped spacing, inconsistent components, weak or mismatched icons, redundant elements, and missing interactive feedback. For each, he shows a concrete fix: sketch the flow first, remove or soften gradients and shadows, align to column grids and use auto layout, give duplicate components one design and one small-component corner radius, use one icon library with labels or tooltips where icons are unclear, cut arrows and strokes that add clutter, and show press and loading states. For a design system, this is a practical review checklist and a set of defaults: fewer effects, more space, shared styles, variables and components, consistent icons, visible feedback, and charts that favour readability over looks.
key_ideas: You can make a UI look polished by fixing specific mistakes one at a time, without starting from scratch.
Planning the user flow, even as boxes sketched on paper, catches gaps such as a missing search bar or skip button before users feel them.
The elements designers most often miss are navigation links, hidden states and dynamic interactions such as button hovers and micro interactions.
Overusing shadows, glows and gradients makes a design feel cluttered and amateur; less visual noise is usually better.
If a gradient is needed, keep it within one color (lighter and darker shades), but no gradient is usually cleaner.
Soften drop shadows by changing the shadow color to a light gray and raising the blur, not just by lowering opacity, or remove them.
Beginner layouts are usually too tight; column grids, more vertical spacing and auto layout fix most of it, and mobile needs more space than you think.
Components that do the same job must look the same, and all smaller components should share one corner radius.
Consistency comes from styles for colors, variables for measurements and components for UI elements.
Good icons speed up browsing and bad or mismatched icons hurt a design; use one library so fill, line width and style match.
Well-known icons can stand alone, but unclear ones need a tooltip; different icon styles can coexist only in visually separate areas with different jobs.
Remove elements that add nothing, such as arrows where people can swipe and strokes that are not needed.
Actions need visible feedback: a grayed-out pressed button, a loading wheel for long waits, and a sign showing where a saved item went.
Charts are often over-designed; a plain chart with an axis carries more useful information than a decorative one.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Lists seven beginner mistakes (flow, effects, spacing, inconsistency, icons, redundancy, feedback) plus over-designed charts, and how to spot and fix each quickly.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Plan the user flow before designing, even by sketching boxes on paper, and improve an existing UI one mistake at a time rather than restarting.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Avoid multi-hue gradients like blue and green; if a gradient is needed use lighter and darker shades of one color, though no gradient is usually cleaner.

topics.name: Depth, shadows and borders
topics.summary: Figma default shadows are too harsh; recolor them to light gray with much more blur, or remove them. Strokes that are not needed should be removed or dimmed significantly.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Beginner UIs are packed too tight; align to three-column and two-column grids, allow slight breaks if balanced, increase vertical spacing in stacks, and use auto layout for cards and chips.

topics.name: Shape and corner radius
topics.summary: Mixed corner radii make a design feel amateur; set all smaller components to one radius (10 pixels in the example).

topics.name: Design systems and tokens
topics.summary: Consistency means styles for colors, variables for measurements and components for UI elements; duplicate components such as back and skip buttons must match.

topics.name: Icons and imagery
topics.summary: Add icons to cards to cut reading, use one icon library so fill, line width and style match, download SVG, label or tooltip unclear icons, and only mix styles in visually separate areas.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Buttons that do the same job must match in size, corner radius and style; gray a button out when pressed so people know it registered; in the example a button's color is dimmed while removing clutter.

topics.name: Feedback, empty and loading states
topics.summary: A short delay with no feedback looks like the tap failed; gray the button out on press and add a loading wheel for long waits.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Hovers and micro interactions are commonly missed; filling the save icon and adding a red dot to the save tab shows people where the saved recipe went.

topics.name: Mobile app patterns
topics.summary: Arrows are redundant where people can swipe on mobile, and mobile screens need more spacing than designers expect.

topics.name: Dashboards and data display
topics.summary: Over-designed charts are hard to read: a chart needs a vertical axis, rounded bar tops hide where bars end, and bar counts should match the data (not 16 bars for 7 days).

topics.name: Figma and design tools
topics.summary: Uses Figma layout grids, auto layout with vertical trim off, styles, variables and components, and icon plugins (Feather, Phosphor).

rules.rule: Plan the user flow before designing screens, even by sketching boxes on paper, and check each screen for gaps.
rules.why: Gaps like a missing search bar or skip button are easy to miss without a plan, but users feel them instantly.
rules.evidence: Mistake number one, user flow

rules.rule: On a screen of preset choices, add a search field for choices not listed and a skip button for people to whom none apply.
rules.why: The allergy screen with six presets had no way to enter another allergy or to say there are none.
rules.evidence: Here's our allergy screen with six preset options

rules.rule: Check every flow for navigation links, hidden states and dynamic interactions such as button hovers and micro interactions.
rules.why: These are the most commonly missed elements; small touches like a filter icon on the search bar or a save button up top go a long way.
rules.evidence: The most commonly missed elements

rules.rule: Don't blend different hues in a gradient (such as blue and green); if a gradient is needed, use lighter and darker shades of one color, and prefer no gradient at all.
rules.why: The blue-green gradient was 'just not working', and the design looks cleaner with no gradient, which is usually the case.
rules.evidence: Let's start with the gradient here

rules.rule: Don't overuse visual effects such as shadows, glows and gradients.
rules.why: Overusing them can make designs feel cluttered and amateur; the description says these mistakes should be avoided at all costs.
rules.evidence: Mistake number two, overusing effects

rules.rule: Don't ship Figma's default drop shadow; change the shadow color to a light gray and increase the blur significantly, instead of only lowering opacity, or remove the shadow.
rules.why: Figma defaults are way too harsh, and less visual noise usually means a better design.
rules.evidence: These Figma defaults are way too harsh

rules.rule: Set up a column grid for each screen (three columns on one screen and two on another in the example) and align elements to it as closely as possible; leave an element that breaks the grid slightly if it still feels balanced.
rules.why: Most beginner UIs are packed way too tight; grids and auto layout are the two tools he uses to fix that.
rules.evidence: First, we'll set up a three column grid

rules.rule: Increase the vertical spacing in stacked content so items breathe and group naturally, and give mobile screens more space than you think they need.
rules.why: Most beginner UIs are packed way too tight.
rules.evidence: for stack content like this, increase the vertical spacing

rules.rule: Build cards and chips with auto layout, turn off vertical trim for pixel-perfect control, and repeat the same spacing across the UI.
rules.why: The card and chip layouts were wonky; auto layout keeps spacing consistent and clean.
rules.evidence: Perfect time to use auto layout

rules.rule: Make components that do the same job identical: the two search bars differ only in prompt text, and the back and skip buttons match in size, corner radius and style.
rules.why: Identical components designed differently make the design feel amateur.
rules.evidence: Mistake number four, inconsistent components

rules.rule: Give all smaller components one shared corner radius (10 pixels in the example) instead of a mix of radii.
rules.why: The design had all sorts of different corner radiuses; this is an important step most designers miss.
rules.evidence: We'll set the corner radius of all smaller components

rules.rule: Use styles for colors, variables for measurements and components for UI elements.
rules.why: That is what being consistent means and it brings the design together.
rules.evidence: Being consistent means using styles for colors

rules.rule: Add icons to content cards and replace short text actions such as 'save' with an icon.
rules.why: Cards with no icons force users to read more and slow down browsing.
rules.evidence: we have no icons on these cards here

rules.rule: Take icons from one library so fill, line width and style match; on the icon website, select interface icons and sort by stroke, width and corner, and download SVG.
rules.why: The top icons were mismatched in fill, line width and style; SVG gives the best results.
rules.evidence: they're mismatched in fill, line width, and style

rules.rule: If you prefer a Figma plugin for icons, Feather Icons and Phosphor Icons are the source's picks.
rules.why: Personal preference offered as an alternative to downloading from an icon website.
rules.evidence: I like feather icons and phosphor icons

rules.rule: Leave well-known icons (house, bookmark, user) without labels, but give less familiar icon-only buttons a tooltip, and avoid bizarre icons.
rules.why: A tooltip for unclear icons makes onboarding much smoother.
rules.evidence: a fair amount of icons down here without labels

rules.rule: Only mix icon styles when each style lives in a visually separate area with a different job (for example navbar icons, food icons and recipe icons).
rules.why: Different styles work together when they are in separate areas and used for different things.
rules.evidence: this is a very pro tip

rules.rule: Remove arrows that people don't need, such as arrows on content they can swipe on mobile or arrows that are just decoration; in the example the button's color is also dimmed.
rules.why: Redundant elements are visual clutter, a common mistake as the trend of having stuff everywhere takes over.
rules.evidence: Mistake number six, redundant elements

rules.rule: Remove strokes on elements that don't need them; if you are worried about contrast ratios, dim them significantly instead.
rules.why: The stroke was really not needed and added clutter.
rules.evidence: the stroke on these elements is really not needed

rules.rule: Gray out a button as soon as it is pressed when the next screen may take a moment to load, and add a loading wheel if it takes a long time.
rules.why: Without feedback it looks like the button was never clicked; graying it out shows the next screen is coming.
rules.evidence: Mistake number seven, interactive feedback

rules.rule: When an item is saved, fill in the save icon and add a red dot to the save tab.
rules.why: It makes clear to the user that a new recipe was added to the save tab.
rules.evidence: Another good example is clicking on this save icon

rules.rule: Give bar charts a vertical axis, avoid rounded bar tops, and make the number of bars match the data (the example had 16 bars for only 7 days of the week).
rules.why: Without an axis the chart is basically impossible to read, rounded tops hide where a bar ends, and extra bars don't match the data.
rules.evidence: Bonus mistake number eight, charts

rules.rule: Prefer a simple, readable chart over a decorative one copied from design showcases.
rules.why: The simple chart is less aesthetic but conveys much more useful information.
rules.evidence: Which one do you think I got from Dribble?

decisions.question: Should the UI use gradients, and if so, what kind?

options.name: No gradient
options.effect: Flat color; looks cleaner with less visual noise.
options.when: Usually; the source says this is usually the case.

options.name: Single-hue gradient
options.effect: Darker and lighter shades of one color (for example green).
options.when: Only if you really need a gradient.

options.name: Multi-hue gradient
options.effect: Blends two different colors such as blue and green; in the example it is just not working.
options.when: The source does not recommend it.

decisions.recommendation: No gradient; if one is really needed, keep it to variations of the same color.
decisions.evidence: Let's start with the gradient here

decisions.question: What should drop shadows look like?

options.name: Figma default shadow
options.effect: Figma's default drop shadow, which the source calls way too harsh.
options.when: Not recommended.

options.name: Soft light-gray shadow
options.effect: Shadow color changed to a light gray with the blur increased significantly.
options.when: When you keep a shadow at all [inferred].

options.name: Lower opacity only
options.effect: Same shadow, just fainter; the source changes the color instead of only lowering opacity.
options.when: Not the source's approach.

options.name: No shadow
options.effect: Flat surface, less visual noise.
options.when: Most of the time.

decisions.recommendation: Recolor to light gray with much more blur, or remove the shadow completely, because less visual noise usually means a better design.
decisions.evidence: Now, let's talk drop shadows for a second

decisions.question: How roomy should screens be?

options.name: Packed tight
options.effect: What most beginner UIs do; elements feel cramped and wonky.
options.when: The source calls this a mistake.

options.name: More generous spacing
options.effect: More vertical space in stacks lets things breathe and group naturally.
options.when: Especially on mobile screens, which need more space than you think.

decisions.recommendation: Increase spacing, especially the vertical spacing of stacked content on mobile.
decisions.evidence: Most beginner UIs are packed way too tight

decisions.question: Should an element that slightly breaks the column grid be forced back into alignment?

options.name: Force it onto the grid
options.effect: Strict alignment everywhere.
options.when: When the break makes the layout feel unbalanced [inferred].

options.name: Leave the slight break
options.effect: Keeps the element as designed while the rest aligns to the grid.
options.when: If it still feels balanced.

decisions.recommendation: Align as closely as possible, but leave a slight break as is if it still feels balanced.
decisions.evidence: If something needs to break the grid slightly

decisions.question: Should smaller components each keep their own corner radius, or share one?

options.name: Mixed radii
options.effect: All sorts of different corner radiuses across the design; feels amateur.
options.when: The source calls this a mistake.

options.name: One shared radius
options.effect: All smaller components use one radius (10 pixels in the example).
options.when: Always, per the source; most designers miss it.

decisions.recommendation: Set all smaller components to one corner radius (10 pixels in the example app).
decisions.evidence: We'll set the corner radius of all smaller components to be 10 pixels

decisions.question: Which icons need a text label?

options.name: No label
options.effect: The icon stands alone; the source says you don't need anything else.
options.when: Well-known icons such as the house, bookmark and user.

options.name: Tooltip pop-up
options.effect: The icon explains itself when needed, making onboarding smoother.
options.when: Icons that are not well known.

decisions.recommendation: Leave well-known icons unlabeled and add a tooltip to less familiar ones; avoid bizarre icons.
decisions.evidence: a fair amount of icons down here without labels

decisions.question: Should every icon in the product share one style?

options.name: One library and one style
options.effect: Matching fill, line width and style; consistent results.
options.when: Within any one area, such as a row of top icons.

options.name: Different styles in separate areas
options.effect: Navbar, food and recipe icons differ slightly but still work together.
options.when: Only when the areas are visually separate and the icons are used for different things.

decisions.recommendation: Use one library so icons match; mixing styles is okay only across visually separate areas with different jobs.
decisions.evidence: it is okay to have different styles of icons

decisions.question: Should navigation arrows stay on swipeable content and buttons?

options.name: Remove the arrow
options.effect: Less visual clutter; people swipe on mobile instead.
options.when: When the content can be swiped, or the arrow is just decoration.

options.name: Keep the arrow
options.effect: An extra visible cue [inferred].
options.when: The source keeps some arrows, while admitting one could argue they aren't needed.

decisions.recommendation: Remove arrows that are redundant or just clutter, and dim the button color.
decisions.evidence: we can get rid of this arrow since we'll be able to swipe on mobile

decisions.question: What should happen to strokes (outlines) on cards and elements?

options.name: Remove them
options.effect: No outline; the source says the stroke is really not needed.
options.when: When the stroke isn't needed; the source's choice.

options.name: Dim them significantly
options.effect: A much fainter outline.
options.when: If you are worried about contrast ratios.

options.name: Keep them as they are
options.effect: Outlines stay as they are.
options.when: The source does not recommend it.

decisions.recommendation: Rip unneeded strokes out; dim them significantly if contrast ratios are a concern.
decisions.evidence: the stroke on these elements is really not needed

decisions.question: What should people see between tapping a button and the next screen appearing?

options.name: Nothing
options.effect: If loading takes a split second, it looks like the button was never clicked.
options.when: Not recommended.

options.name: Grayed-out button
options.effect: The button changes on tap, showing the next screen is coming.
options.when: Any navigation step that may take a moment.

options.name: Loading wheel
options.effect: An explicit sign that work is happening.
options.when: If it is really taking a long time.

decisions.recommendation: Gray the button out on tap, and add a loading wheel for long waits.
decisions.evidence: if we make it grayed out when we click on it

decisions.question: Should charts be simple and readable or decorative?

options.name: Simple chart
options.effect: Has an axis and plain bars; less aesthetic but conveys much more useful information.
options.when: Whenever people need to read the data.

options.name: Decorative showcase chart
options.effect: No vertical axis, rounded bar tops, 16 bars for 7 days; basically impossible to read.
options.when: The source does not recommend it.

decisions.recommendation: The simple chart, because it conveys more useful information.

process.detail: Take the existing design and fix one mistake at a time until it looks polished, instead of starting from scratch.
Sketch the screens as boxes on paper and look for gaps such as a missing search or skip option, missing navigation links, hidden states and hover or micro interactions.
Remove multi-hue gradients (or keep one-color ones), and recolor harsh default shadows to light gray with more blur, or remove them.
Set up column grids, align elements to them, increase vertical spacing in stacks, and rebuild cards and chips with auto layout with vertical trim off.
Make duplicate components identical, give smaller components one corner radius, and use styles for colors, variables for measurements and components for UI elements.
Add icons where text slows browsing, take them from one library as SVG, and add tooltips to icons that aren't well known.
Delete arrows people don't need and strokes that add nothing, dimming instead where contrast is a concern.
Show a pressed or grayed-out state on tap, a loading wheel for long waits, and a sign of where a saved item went.
Make sure charts have an axis, bars whose ends are clear, and one bar per data point.

caveats: Opinion and experience of one designer, shown on a single recipe app; the fixes are his judgement calls, not tested rules.
The grid measurements are shown on screen but not stated in the transcript, so no column, gutter or margin values could be extracted.
The 10 pixel radius is the value chosen for this app; the lasting lesson is one shared radius for smaller components [inferred].
Icon sources (the site heard as 'flat icons', taken to be Flaticon; Feather and Phosphor plugins) are personal preferences.
Removing strokes can lower contrast; the source itself offers dimming as the option when contrast ratios are a concern.
Self-promotion: the Figma file is behind a link to his own site, and he points to his separate video on interactive feedback and micro interactions.
Published June 2025; Figma features mentioned (auto layout, vertical trim, styles, variables) are as of that date.
Auto-captions without visuals: the before/after images are described only from the narration; no media list was available.
